chapters.title: Acts 1 — The risen Jesus ascends and the disciples await the Spirit
chapters.historicalContext: Acts opens as a continuation of Luke’s Gospel. The risen Jesus teaches the disciples about God’s kingdom, ascends from their sight, and promises the Spirit. The community returns to Jerusalem, prays, and chooses Matthias to join the Twelve.
chapters.overview: The chapter bridges the ministry of Jesus and the witness of the church. The disciples are told to wait for the Spirit and to become witnesses from Jerusalem outward, while prayer and shared discernment shape the community.
chapters.studyObservation: The question about restoring the kingdom of Israel reflects the disciples’ hopes, while Jesus redirects them toward Spirit-empowered witness. The ascension marks a transition in the story, not Jesus’ abandonment of his followers.
chapters.connectionNotes: Read Acts 1 alongside Luke 24 and the biblical hope for God’s reign. The choice of Matthias shows the community seeking continuity and shared responsibility after Judas’ betrayal.
chapters.lifeApplication: Wait with prayerful expectation, seek wise communal discernment, and understand witness as faithful testimony rather than self-promotion or coercion.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The promise of power is for witness, not domination. The chapter does not authorise leaders to claim unquestionable authority or to force people into religious participation.
chapters.readingNote: Follow the movement from Jesus’ final teaching to the ascension and the community’s prayer. Notice the promise of the Spirit and the geographical scope of the coming witness.
studyQuestions: What does Jesus say the Spirit will empower the disciples to do?
How does the ascension change the disciples’ task without ending Jesus’ work?
What does the choice of Matthias reveal about communal discernment?

chapters.title: Acts 2 — Pentecost, Peter’s message, and the first community
chapters.historicalContext: On the day of Pentecost, the Spirit comes upon the gathered disciples, and people from many regions hear the message in their own languages. Peter explains the event through Scripture, proclaims Jesus’ resurrection, and many are baptised and join the community.
chapters.overview: The chapter presents the Spirit as the source of a multilingual witness that crosses boundaries. The new community devotes itself to teaching, fellowship, shared meals, prayer, and practical care.
chapters.studyObservation: Peter interprets Pentecost through Joel and the Psalms, placing the event within Israel’s scriptural hope. The shared life of the believers is described as voluntary generosity and mutual support.
chapters.connectionNotes: The languages and nations list signals a widening mission without erasing cultural difference. The community’s sharing should be read in its historical setting and alongside the later account of individual stewardship.
chapters.lifeApplication: Make room for people from different backgrounds to hear and participate. Practise generosity freely, remain devoted to learning and prayer, and let faith create practical care.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The sharing of possessions is not a mandate for forced communal ownership or coercive fundraising. Do not use the crowd’s response to shame people who need time to understand or make a decision.
chapters.readingNote: Notice how the Spirit’s arrival leads to public witness, Peter’s scriptural explanation, and the formation of a community. The chapter connects spiritual experience with teaching, fellowship, and daily care.
studyQuestions: Why is it significant that people hear the message in their own languages?
How does Peter connect Pentecost with Israel’s Scriptures?
What practices shape the life of the first community?

chapters.title: Acts 3 — A man is healed at the temple gate
chapters.historicalContext: Peter and John meet a man who has been unable to walk from birth at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. In Jesus’ name he is healed, and the crowd gathers as Peter explains the sign and calls listeners to turn toward God.
chapters.overview: The healing becomes an occasion for public witness to Jesus’ resurrection and power. Peter directs attention away from the apostles’ own ability and toward the God who has glorified Jesus.
chapters.studyObservation: The setting at the temple shows continuity with Jewish worship and prayer. Peter’s message interprets the sign through the prophets and the hope of restoration.
chapters.connectionNotes: The man’s disability is not presented as a moral failure. Peter’s speech is a Jewish proclamation within a Jewish setting and must not be turned into collective blame of Jewish people.
chapters.lifeApplication: Notice people who are often overlooked and offer practical care with dignity. When good things happen through your service, direct gratitude toward God rather than claiming personal greatness.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not use this healing to blame people who remain disabled or to promise that every condition will be cured immediately. The apostles’ witness is not a licence for spectacle or manipulation.
chapters.readingNote: Read the healing before Peter’s explanation. Ask how the sign directs attention to Jesus and how the temple setting shapes the audience’s response.
studyQuestions: How does Peter redirect attention from the apostles to Jesus?
Why does the temple setting matter for the story?
How can churches offer care without blaming people whose conditions do not change?

chapters.title: Acts 4 — The apostles face opposition and the community shares generously
chapters.historicalContext: Peter and John are questioned by the authorities after the healing and speak boldly about Jesus. The believers pray for courage, and the community shares resources so that people in need are supported.
chapters.overview: The chapter contrasts institutional pressure with Spirit-given courage and mutual care. The community’s generosity responds to real needs, while the apostles continue to speak openly about Jesus.
chapters.studyObservation: The prayer draws on Psalm 2 and interprets opposition within the larger story of God’s purposes. Barnabas’ gift illustrates voluntary generosity and becomes a contrast with later deception.
chapters.connectionNotes: The conflict takes place among Jewish leaders and followers of Jesus in the early Jewish movement. It must not be used to portray Jewish people collectively as opponents of the Gospel.
chapters.lifeApplication: Speak truth with courage and respect, support people facing hardship, and give freely without seeking status. Let prayer strengthen faithful action rather than replace it.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Generosity in this chapter is voluntary. It does not authorise leaders to control private property, pressure vulnerable people, or punish those who cannot give.
chapters.readingNote: Follow the apostles’ hearing, their prayer after release, and the community’s shared resources. Notice how courage and practical care belong together.
studyQuestions: How do Peter and John explain the source of their authority?
What does the community ask for when it prays under pressure?
How does Barnabas’ generosity model voluntary care?

chapters.title: Acts 5 — Ananias and Sapphira, signs, and the apostles’ witness
chapters.historicalContext: Ananias and Sapphira misrepresent a gift and die after being confronted by Peter. The apostles continue healing and teaching, are arrested, and are brought before the council, where they insist that obedience to God takes priority.
chapters.overview: The chapter presents a serious warning about deception and the misuse of spiritual trust. It also shows the apostles continuing their witness despite threats and imprisonment.
chapters.studyObservation: The story of Ananias and Sapphira concerns deliberate deceit, not the failure to donate all possessions. Gamaliel’s counsel later urges restraint and warns against claiming certainty about every movement.
chapters.connectionNotes: Read the account within the early community’s concern for truthful stewardship. The deaths are narrated as a unique event and should not be used to threaten people who disagree with leaders.
chapters.lifeApplication: Practise honesty in giving and leadership, and make room for accountability. When facing pressure, seek courage to do what is right without becoming reckless or contemptuous.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Peter’s confrontation is not permission for spiritual leaders to threaten or harm people. The passage must never be used to justify financial coercion, fear-based control, or claims that illness and death prove divine punishment.
chapters.readingNote: Notice the contrast between the community’s shared trust and the deception in the opening story. Then follow the apostles’ continued witness and the council’s debate about how to respond.
studyQuestions: What is the difference between voluntary giving and the deception in this account?
How do the apostles respond to threats from the council?
What wisdom does Gamaliel offer about judging a movement?

chapters.title: Acts 6 — The community appoints servants and Stephen is accused
chapters.historicalContext: A dispute arises because some widows are overlooked in the daily distribution. The apostles invite the community to appoint trusted people to oversee the practical work, and Stephen, full of faith and the Spirit, becomes a prominent witness who is later accused.
chapters.overview: The chapter shows the church responding to inequity by changing its structures and sharing responsibility. Practical service and public witness are both important to the community’s mission.
chapters.studyObservation: The neglected widows are associated with the Greek-speaking group, showing that cultural and language differences can create unequal treatment. The appointment process seeks trust, wisdom, and accountability.
chapters.connectionNotes: The selection of servants is a response to a real distribution problem, not a rigid blueprint that excludes other forms of leadership. Stephen’s opponents belong to particular groups in the story, not to Jewish people as a whole.
chapters.lifeApplication: Pay attention to who is being overlooked in shared resources and decision-making. Build systems that are fair, transparent, and responsive to people who lack influence.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not spiritualise unequal treatment or ask disadvantaged people simply to endure neglect. The chapter models practical correction and shared responsibility.
chapters.readingNote: Read the complaint about widows as a turning point in the community’s organisation. Notice how addressing practical injustice makes room for the word to continue spreading.
studyQuestions: Why did the daily distribution need to change?
What qualities were sought in those appointed to serve?
How can communities identify and correct patterns of exclusion?

chapters.title: Acts 7 — Stephen’s speech and his death as a witness
chapters.historicalContext: Stephen responds to accusations with a long retelling of Israel’s history, from Abraham through Moses and the prophets. He challenges the leaders’ resistance to God’s messengers, sees a vision of Jesus, and is killed by stoning as Saul looks on.
chapters.overview: Stephen’s speech interprets the present conflict through Israel’s own story and prophetic tradition. His death exposes the cost of witness and introduces Saul, whose later transformation will shape Acts.
chapters.studyObservation: The speech recalls both God’s faithfulness and repeated resistance to prophetic voices. Stephen’s final words echo Jesus’ prayer for forgiveness and entrustment to God.
chapters.connectionNotes: Stephen is a Jewish follower of Jesus speaking within Israel’s history. His critique must not be used to condemn Jewish people collectively or to erase the Jewish roots of the early church.
chapters.lifeApplication: Remain truthful under pressure, remember the wider story of God’s faithfulness, and resist retaliation. Let forgiveness shape your response without denying the seriousness of violence.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Stephen’s martyrdom does not glorify persecution or require people to remain in danger. The account must never be used to justify violence against any religious group.
chapters.readingNote: Follow the speech as a carefully structured retelling of Israel’s story. Notice how Stephen connects the ancestors, Moses, the prophets, and the present response to Jesus.
studyQuestions: How does Stephen use Israel’s history to answer the accusations?
What does his final prayer echo from Jesus’ words on the cross?
Why must Stephen’s critique not become collective blame of Jewish people?

chapters.title: Acts 8 — The message spreads to Samaria and an Ethiopian official
chapters.historicalContext: After persecution scatters believers from Jerusalem, Philip proclaims the message in Samaria and encounters Simon, who seeks spiritual power for profit. Later, Philip meets an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah and explains the good news about Jesus.
chapters.overview: The chapter shows the message crossing geographic, ethnic, and social boundaries. The Spirit guides the mission, and the Ethiopian official becomes a witness after hearing and responding to the message.
chapters.studyObservation: The Samaritans share scriptural roots with Judeans amid long-standing tensions. The Ethiopian official’s inclusion signals the widening reach of the Gospel and the importance of interpreting Scripture in conversation.
chapters.connectionNotes: Simon’s desire to purchase spiritual authority is a warning against commodifying ministry. The Ethiopian official’s identity should not be reduced to a stereotype; the narrative highlights his agency and faith.
chapters.lifeApplication: Welcome people across boundaries, share Scripture in ways that answer real questions, and refuse to turn spiritual gifts into products for sale.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not use Simon’s story to label people who ask questions as malicious. Baptism and inclusion must not be used to pressure people or ignore their dignity and agency.
chapters.readingNote: Notice how scattering becomes an unexpected route for the message to spread. Compare the Samaria account with Philip’s encounter on the road and the official’s response to Isaiah.
studyQuestions: How does the message cross the boundary between Judea and Samaria?
What does Simon’s request reveal about the danger of treating spiritual power as a commodity?
How does Philip help the Ethiopian official understand Isaiah?

chapters.title: Acts 9 — Saul encounters Jesus and becomes a witness
chapters.historicalContext: Saul travels toward Damascus to arrest followers of Jesus but is confronted by a heavenly light and the voice of Jesus. Ananias is sent to him, Saul receives his sight and is baptised, and his preaching leads to opposition and escape.
chapters.overview: The chapter portrays a dramatic reversal in Saul’s life and the beginning of his mission as a witness to Jesus. Ananias’ obedience and the believers’ cautious welcome show that transformation involves community as well as personal encounter.
chapters.studyObservation: Saul’s encounter connects the risen Jesus with the people he persecutes. The story emphasises both divine initiative and the role of Ananias, who must overcome fear to help Saul.
chapters.connectionNotes: The narrative does not erase the harm Saul caused or suggest that victims must immediately trust someone who has harmed them. The community’s caution is understandable and remains part of the story.
chapters.lifeApplication: Be open to genuine transformation while keeping wise safeguards. Offer support to people taking new steps toward faithfulness, and do not pressure those harmed to rush reconciliation.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: A conversion story is not proof that accountability is unnecessary. People who have been harmed are not obligated to restore trust without evidence of change and appropriate protection.
chapters.readingNote: Follow the parallel roles of Saul and Ananias. The chapter shows that a changed direction requires both personal response and the courage of a community willing to discern and support.
studyQuestions: How does Jesus identify with the people Saul is persecuting?
What does Ananias risk by obeying the instruction to visit Saul?
How can communities welcome change while still protecting people who were harmed?

chapters.title: Acts 10 — Peter and Cornelius: the Spirit welcomes Gentiles
chapters.historicalContext: Cornelius, a Roman centurion who seeks God, receives a vision and sends for Peter. Peter sees a vision about clean and unclean animals, visits Cornelius, proclaims Jesus, and witnesses the Spirit coming upon Gentile listeners before they are baptised.
chapters.overview: The chapter marks a major turning point in Acts as Gentiles receive the Spirit without first becoming Jews. Peter learns that God shows no partiality and that the message of Jesus is for all who respond.
chapters.studyObservation: The visions prepare both Cornelius and Peter for an encounter that challenges inherited boundaries. The Spirit’s arrival confirms God’s initiative and leads the community to recognise Gentile inclusion.
chapters.connectionNotes: The vision should not be reduced to a simplistic rejection of Jewish dietary practice; Peter interprets it in relation to people and inclusion. Cornelius’ Roman military role is part of the historical setting, not a blanket endorsement of empire.
chapters.lifeApplication: Examine assumptions that limit who can belong, listen for the Spirit’s work beyond familiar settings, and welcome people with dignity while learning from one another.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The story does not demand that people abandon cultural identity to be included. Nor does it make every institution or occupation morally neutral; the focus is God’s welcome and the Spirit’s initiative.
chapters.readingNote: Read the two visions together before Peter’s speech. Notice how the Spirit’s arrival changes the question from whether Gentiles may be welcomed to how the community should respond to what God has done.
studyQuestions: How do the visions prepare Cornelius and Peter for their meeting?
What does Peter learn about partiality and inclusion?
Why does the Spirit’s arrival matter before the Gentiles are baptised?

chapters.title: Acts 11 — Peter explains Gentile inclusion and Antioch becomes a centre
chapters.historicalContext: Peter explains to believers in Jerusalem why he entered a Gentile home and how the Spirit came upon Cornelius’ household. The message spreads to Antioch, where a diverse community grows and Barnabas brings Saul to help teach.
chapters.overview: The chapter shows the church learning to recognise God’s work across boundaries. Antioch becomes a significant centre where disciples are first called Christians and where generosity is organised for believers facing famine.
chapters.studyObservation: Peter’s account emphasises that the Spirit came upon Gentiles just as upon the Jewish disciples at Pentecost. The Antioch community brings together people from different backgrounds and gifts.
chapters.connectionNotes: The debate is an internal discussion among early followers of Jesus about Gentile inclusion. It should not be framed as hostility between separate religions or used to erase the Jewish identity of the earliest believers.
chapters.lifeApplication: Listen carefully when people describe how God has worked beyond your expectations. Build communities where different backgrounds contribute, and respond to hardship through practical support.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Inclusion does not require cultural erasure or pressure to assimilate. Generosity should be voluntary and organised with accountability.
chapters.readingNote: Follow Peter’s explanation from Jerusalem to the growth of Antioch. Notice how recognition of the Spirit’s work leads to wider fellowship and practical care across regions.
studyQuestions: What persuades the Jerusalem believers that God has welcomed Gentiles?
What makes the Antioch community significant in the story?
How does the community respond to the famine warning?

chapters.title: Acts 12 — Peter is freed and the word continues to spread
chapters.historicalContext: Herod arrests members of the church, and James the brother of John is executed. Peter is imprisoned but an angel leads him out, and he joins the praying community. Herod later dies after accepting public honour, while the word of God continues to grow.
chapters.overview: The chapter contrasts political power and public acclaim with the enduring spread of God’s word. Peter’s escape is a dramatic deliverance, while James’ death reminds readers that faithful people do not all experience the same outcome.
chapters.studyObservation: The narrative places the church’s prayer alongside both deliverance and loss. Herod’s downfall echoes biblical warnings against rulers who claim honour that belongs to God.
chapters.connectionNotes: The death of James must not be explained away or used to promise that every believer will escape persecution. The account reflects the political violence of the period and the vulnerability of the early church.
chapters.lifeApplication: Pray for people facing danger, remember those who suffer, and use influence with humility. Hold hope without judging people whose circumstances do not change.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not imply that James lacked faith because he was killed or that prayer guarantees rescue in every crisis. The passage must not be used to shame people who grieve or to glorify political violence.
chapters.readingNote: Read Peter’s escape alongside the earlier execution of James. The contrast is deliberate: the church’s hope rests in God, not in a guarantee of identical outcomes for every witness.
studyQuestions: What contrast does the chapter establish between James and Peter?
How does the praying community respond when Peter arrives?
What warning about power and honour appears in Herod’s downfall?

chapters.title: Acts 13 — The first missionary journey begins in Cyprus and Pisidian Antioch
chapters.historicalContext: The church at Antioch sends Barnabas and Saul after prayer and fasting. They travel to Cyprus, where Elymas opposes their message, and then to Pisidian Antioch, where Paul explains Israel’s history and proclaims Jesus as the risen Saviour.
chapters.overview: The chapter begins a new phase of the mission beyond Jerusalem. The Spirit directs the sending, and Paul’s message presents Jesus as the fulfilment of God’s promises while inviting a broad response.
chapters.studyObservation: The commissioning comes from a diverse worshipping community that listens and acts together. Paul’s speech follows the pattern of Israel’s story and connects Davidic hope with Jesus’ resurrection.
chapters.connectionNotes: The disputes in the synagogue occur within a Jewish setting and should not be turned into anti-Jewish claims. Paul and Barnabas are Jewish followers of Jesus speaking from Israel’s Scriptures.
chapters.lifeApplication: Support mission through prayer, shared responsibility, and wise discernment. Explain faith in ways that respect the Scriptures and histories of the people listening.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The mission narrative does not justify forced conversion, cultural domination, or contempt for those who disagree. The Spirit’s guidance is discerned in community, not claimed as a licence for coercion.
chapters.readingNote: Notice how the Antioch community sends Barnabas and Saul and how the mission develops through different audiences. Paul’s sermon is a key example of explaining Jesus through Israel’s story.
studyQuestions: What does the Antioch community do before sending Barnabas and Saul?
How does Paul connect Israel’s history with Jesus’ resurrection?
How can Christian witness remain respectful of people who disagree?

chapters.title: Acts 14 — The mission continues through opposition and encouragement
chapters.historicalContext: Paul and Barnabas preach in Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe. In Lystra, a healing leads the crowd to mistake them for gods, but opponents later turn the crowd against Paul. The missionaries continue strengthening new disciples and appointing elders before returning to Antioch.
chapters.overview: The chapter shows the mission bringing both response and resistance. The apostles reject worship directed toward themselves, encourage new believers, and strengthen communities so the work can continue beyond their visit.
chapters.studyObservation: The crowd’s reaction in Lystra reflects local religious expectations, while Paul’s speech points to the Creator’s generosity through rain and fruitful seasons. The return journey shows intentional care for newly formed communities.
chapters.connectionNotes: The appointment of elders is a form of local responsibility and should not be used to claim that one modern leadership model is the only possible arrangement. Opposition must not be interpreted as proof that a mission is automatically right.
chapters.lifeApplication: Refuse personal glorification, build local capacity, and strengthen people through encouragement and practical teaching. Continue serving with courage while recognising real risks.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not romanticise persecution or pressure people to endure avoidable danger. Mission must never become cultural coercion or exploitation of local communities.
chapters.readingNote: Follow the pattern of preaching, response, opposition, and return to strengthen new communities. The chapter closes with a report of what God has done among the nations.
studyQuestions: Why do Paul and Barnabas refuse the crowd’s attempt to worship them?
What does Paul’s speech in Lystra reveal about God’s care for creation?
Why do the missionaries return to strengthen the new communities?
